flags.title: Four editions of this publication are published under one domain; only the root one is in the sitemap
flags.detail: This repository publishes four separate reader-facing editions under the same domain and the same tracking ID: the root publication (ShopNow Kitchen), /editorial/, /counter/ (Crisp & Counter), /counterwise/ and /crisp-index/, with frozen earlier editions under /legacy/. Only the root publication is listed in sitemap.xml; the others are kept out of the root sitemap and are disallowed for crawling in the root robots.txt; only /editorial/ ships a noindex tag today, and robots.txt is not an indexing control at all (FLG-036), and they are all reachable from the single archive page. Google states that scaled content abuse includes "pages without unique content or purpose" and site reputation abuse covers "many low-quality pages"; several near-identical editions of the same five products on one domain is the pattern those policies describe. The root publication is the one that is indexed, and the others are preserved rather than deleted, so the owner can publish any of them on its own domain later if that is preferred.
flags.impact: Five near-identical editions on one domain split the search signals and the tracking data. The fix applied here is one indexed site plus a labelled archive; the owner can reverse it for any edition.
flags.manual_step: Decide which single edition is the product, and whether the other three should stay on this domain at all. Suggestion S-11 records the options; each edition keeps its own generator and gate, so republishing one is a one-line change.

flags.title: The tracking ID's shape does not match the example format in the policy, which is not the same as being wrong
flags.detail: Participation Requirements §2(b) gives the tag format as "XXXXX-##, or such other format as we may designate". The supplied ID shopnow047c-20 has an eleven-character prefix rather than five, and a two-digit suffix that does match. Because the clause expressly allows other designated formats, the shape proves nothing either way: it cannot confirm the ID is valid and it cannot show it is invalid. Recorded so nobody later reads the eleven-character prefix as evidence of a problem, and so the weaker argument - an Associates help page saying IDs end in -20 - is not mistaken for the policy text. Separately §1(g) bars any Amazon trademark or variant in a tag or Associates ID; shopnow047c contains none, which is a genuine pass.
flags.impact: None on its own. It narrows what may be concluded from the ID's appearance and leaves ownership unconfirmed.
flags.manual_step: Export the tracking-ID list from Associates Central and confirm shopnow047c-20 appears on it; that closes this flag and FLG-011 together.

flags.title: The published site carried no privacy notice while loading a click counter on every page
flags.detail: Participation Requirements §3(e) makes the Associate responsible for disclosing "either through a privacy policy or otherwise, the use of cookies, pixels, and other technologies by you and third parties and how you collect, use, store, and disclose data collected from visitors". For most of this repository's history the site loaded assets/analytics.js on every page with no notice anywhere on the live surface; privacy pages existed only under legacy/, belonging to superseded editions.
flags.impact: A disclosure obligation under the Associates policies that was unmet, and a reader-facing gap: nobody could tell what a page they were reading was doing.

This session's separately written draft was dropped in the merge rather than kept as a second privacy page. What remains open is Q-16: whether the shipped wording is adequate where the site is operated from, which is a question for the owner or counsel rather than a build session.

flags.title: The site's own findability claim overstated what robots.txt can do, and two editions were left indexable
flags.detail: The /flagged/ page asserted that the non-root editions are excluded from the index 'through robots.txt and noindex metadata'. Two things are wrong in that sentence, both read from Google's own documentation. First, robots.txt is not an indexing control: 'A robots.txt file tells search engine crawlers which URLs the crawler can access on your site... it is not a mechanism for keeping a web page out of Google' (S24). Second, noindex has to be a meta tag or an HTTP header - 'Specifying the noindex rule in the robots.txt file is not supported by Google' (S25). Meanwhile the shipped files show /editorial/ does carry a noindex tag and /counter/, /counterwise/ and /crisp-index/ do not, while /counter/ and /counterwise/ each advertise a sitemap of their own. So five reader-facing editions of the same five products are crawlable and indexable on one host, which is the duplicate pattern Google's spam policies describe (S09). What this session changed: the root robots.txt now also disallows the two editions it previously left open, and the claim above is worded to match what that actually achieves. What it cannot change from the root publication: a Disallow line only manages crawling, and a noindex tag placed behind a Disallow line cannot be seen at all (S25).
flags.impact: Search engines may surface near-duplicate editions of the same content under the same tracking ID, diluting the one site this project is trying to get ranked.
flags.manual_step: Owner decision, in order of effectiveness: (1) publish the other editions on their own hosts, (2) keep them here but give each one a <meta name="robots" content="noindex,follow"> in its own generator and remove its Disallow line so the tag can be seen (S25), or (3) move them under /legacy/ and treat them as frozen. Each edition is generated by its own tool, so the change belongs to those sessions' files; a request is logged in COORDINATION.md. After any of the three, submit the root sitemap.xml only, in Search Console.

flags.title: Amazon listing pages could not be re-fetched in the latest verification round
flags.detail: Three sessions have now read the five observed listings and each time the titles matched the register character for character. In the most recent round (2026-11-20, session b7320829-affil3) direct fetches of amazon.com failed outright - three attempts on /dp/B0CDY277D3 and one of the five short links - so that round could not re-derive a single listing value. The observed_title, observed_breadcrumb and observed ASIN fields are therefore carried from the dated rounds in data/observations/, not re-confirmed today. That is a limitation of an unauthenticated fetch, not evidence that any value changed: listing copy, prices and included accessories are known to change without notice, which is why no price, rating or accessory count is published anywhere on the site (S03, FLG-016).
flags.impact: Readers can act on the specification grids, but the exact wording of a listing title is a snapshot of a page that can change on any day.
flags.manual_step: Paste each tagged link into a signed-in browser once a month and note whether the title and the included accessories still match the row. Five minutes, and it is the only check that can see the same page a shopper sees.

flags.title: The publishing-workflow page credited the cadence proposal to the wrong suggestion
flags.detail: The workflow page described the two-week guide cadence as 'suggestion S-02 option A'. In this board S-02 is the buy-button decision; the publishing cadence is S-05, whose option C is the pre-review batch the same sentence referred to. Corrected to S-05. It is the third citation defect found by hand in one day, alongside FLG-037 and FLG-038, which is why this session added a citation-integrity check to the publishing gate (S-25): every S-id, FLG-id and S-id token inside a register string now has to resolve to a real row, so the next mis-numbered reference fails the build instead of shipping.
flags.impact: A reader following the citation lands on a different decision, and the decision it points at (buy buttons) is the one with money attached.
flags.resolution: Wording corrected in tools/build.mjs by session b7320829-affil3 on 2026-11-20, and the gate now checks cross-references across the registers.

flags.title: The README documented a published /docs/ surface that is gitignored and was never deployed
flags.detail: README.md's 'What is published' table listed /docs/ as a third, independently generated publication, and its build instructions told a reader to check docs/sitemap.xml. .gitignore carries an explicit '/docs/' entry, and git ls-files confirms zero tracked files under docs/, so nothing in that path is committed and GitHub Pages cannot serve it. The surface the row described exists only in a working copy: its tooling (scripts/, server/) is tracked, its output is not. Corrected on 2026-11-20 by labelling it as local-only and by listing the surfaces that really are online, which include /counter/ and /counterwise/, previously unlisted in that table. This is the same class of drift as the indexability claim in FLG-036: documentation describing an intention rather than the shipped tree.
flags.impact: Anyone auditing the repository from the README looks for a publication at a URL that returns 404, and may conclude a verification pass was lost rather than never deployed.
flags.resolution: README corrected by session b7320829-affil3, which listed the tracked surfaces, marked the docs site as local-only, and refreshed the gate counts to the numbers this branch's gate reports.
flags.manual_step: If the /docs/ publication is wanted live, its output must be generated into a tracked path (or published from a workflow); the alternative is to treat scripts/ and server/ as tooling for the root site and say so.
